research.title: Alice & Bob: about 22,600 'cat qubits' could break RSA-2048 encryption in about 3 days, on paper
research.who: Alice & Bob (private, France) with Inria, CEA and the University of Edinburgh
research.found: A preprint (IACR ePrint 2026/2665) maps Shor's code-breaking algorithm all the way down to a physical chip layout. It estimates RSA-2048 could be factored with 22,593 physical cat qubits in 3.14 days, about 40 times fewer physical qubits than leading estimates for standard (transmon) qubits and less than half the team's own 2023 figure of 49,649. For the 256-bit elliptic-curve keys used by Bitcoin it estimates up to 29,588 qubits and about 62 minutes.
research.analogy: Like an engineer publishing full blueprints showing a bridge needs 40 times fewer steel beams than everyone assumed: the bridge is not built yet, but the cost estimate just shrank.
research.brief: This is a paper estimate, not a working machine. It assumes hardware that does not exist yet (1-microsecond error-correction cycles and almost no bit-flip errors); with hourly bit-flips the machine grows to about 45,000 qubits. Each such cut shortens the safe window for today's encryption. US NIST and the UK NCSC direct critical systems to move to post-quantum encryption by 2035.
win: Post-quantum security chip and software vendors (our judgment)
Cat-qubit hardware makers, if the hardware follows (our judgment)
research.watch: Peer review of the preprint and Alice & Bob hardware milestones toward error-corrected cat qubits.
research.eli10: Scientists worked out that a future quantum computer may need far fewer parts than expected to crack the locks that protect bank websites, so those locks need upgrading sooner.
tm: 1 yr (our judgment): Banks and governments speed up post-quantum upgrades
3 yr (our judgment): First small error-corrected cat-qubit demos
5 yr+ (our judgment): Machines of this size remain uncertain
bear: Estimate rests on hardware assumptions not yet demonstrated
Alice & Bob is private; listed exposure is indirect (our judgment)
research.ip: Quantum error-correction patents are crowded; no known dispute. (our judgment)

research.title: ISRO's GSLV-F18 puts NVS-03 in orbit, set to restore India's own GPS (NavIC)
research.found: GSLV-F18 lifted off from Sriharikota at 11:51 pm IST on Oct 30 and placed the 2,250 kg NVS-03 satellite in a transfer orbit about 18 minutes later. It carries an Indian-made atomic clock plus bought-in clocks, and adds the L1 signal that common phone chips already use. ISRO's chairman said the launch restores the minimum four satellites NavIC needs for positioning; it had only three working after NVS-02 failed to reach its orbit in 2025.
research.analogy: Like lighthouses along a coast: a ship needs to see at least four lights to fix its position. One light had gone dark, and this launch relights it.
research.brief: NavIC is India's regional navigation system, covering India and about 1,500 km around it. Without four working satellites it could not give positions on its own (timing still worked). The new L1 signal makes NavIC easier to use in everyday phones. The satellite still has to raise itself to its final orbit and be commissioned; NVS-04 and NVS-05 are in advanced stages.

Phone, car and chip makers adding NavIC L1 support (our judgment)
research.watch: Orbit-raising and commissioning of NVS-03; launch dates for NVS-04/05; ISRO's next launches this financial year.
research.eli10: India launched a new satellite for its own map-and-location system, so phones and ships in India can rely less on America's GPS.
tm: 1 yr (our judgment): NVS-03 commissioned; standalone NavIC positioning back
3 yr (our judgment): NVS-04/05 complete the new series
5 yr (our judgment): NavIC common in Indian phones and vehicles
bear: Orbit-raising is the step where NVS-02 failed in 2025
Listed suppliers earn only a small part of revenue from ISRO (our judgment)

research.title: FDA draft rule would let one approval cover many personalised gene-editing treatments
research.found: FDA's draft guidance creates an 'Individualized Feature Space': pre-set limits on how a gene-editing therapy may differ from patient to patient while staying inside one Biologics License Application. If a new patient-specific version stays inside those limits and lab tests show adequate safety and activity, it can be added without new clinical trials. Public comments are open until Nov 27, 2026. CMS also plans to widen its Cell and Gene Therapy Access Model.
research.analogy: Like a tailor approved once for a suit pattern who can then cut each customer's size without a fresh approval, as long as the measurements stay inside the approved range.
research.brief: Until now, a custom edit for one family's ultra-rare mutation looked like a brand-new drug needing its own trials, which is unaffordable for tiny patient groups. This is a draft and non-binding; the final version may change.

research.watch: Final guidance after the Nov 27 comment deadline, and the first application filed under this framework.

research.title: China's DF1000 AI chip stacks memory directly on its logic, reaching 6.4 TB/s without HBM
research.found: At the Chip China expo in Shanghai, Dongfang Suanxin said it delivered the first fully domestic training cluster built on its DF1000 chip: 128 cards ran 72 hours without a stop and adapted the 130-billion-parameter Step 130B model in 7 days. The chip bonds a memory (DRAM) wafer straight onto the logic wafer, copper to copper, with no bumps or interposer. The company claims 6.4 TB/s memory bandwidth and 520 TFLOPS (BF16) on an older 14nm process, and plans a 1,000-card cluster by end-2026.
research.analogy: Like building the warehouse directly above the shop floor, linked by thousands of lifts, instead of trucking goods in from a depot across town.
research.brief: Today's AI chips sit beside stacks of HBM memory, and the link between them is a bottleneck; HBM is also scarce and restricted for Chinese buyers. DF1000 swaps leading-edge transistors for a much shorter, denser memory link. All performance figures are company claims; no independent benchmark yet.

Chinese AI cloud operators seeking non-HBM supply (our judgment)
research.watch: Delivery of the planned 1,000-card cluster by end-2026 and any independent benchmark.
research.eli10: A Chinese company put the chip's memory right on top of its brain, so data travels a tiny distance and the chip does not need hard-to-buy memory.
tm: 1 yr (our judgment): 1,000-card clusters tested
3 yr (our judgment): Memory-on-logic stacking spreads to more AI chips
5 yr (our judgment): Could reduce HBM's role in some inference chips
bear: Performance figures are company claims, not independent tests
Private company; no direct listed exposure (our judgment)

research.title: Mistral releases the weights of Large 4, a ~1-trillion-parameter open model aimed at coding and cyber defence
links: Mistral AI: Large 4 is now open weight (Oct 2026)
research.found: Mistral made the weights of Mistral Large 4 ('Le Chonk') free to download after a preview that began Oct 6. Mistral says it leads open-weight models on Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0 (19.7%) and Terminal-Bench 4.0 (41%), scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and refuses 96.6% of malicious cyber requests on average. API price: $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output tokens. Anyone may use and modify it, but companies selling it as a hosted service need a separate licence. It is also offered through Microsoft Foundry and NVIDIA NIM.
research.analogy: Like a carmaker publishing its full engine design so any garage can build and tune the engine, while taxi companies selling rides with it need a separate licence.
research.brief: Most top models can only be rented through an online service. Open weights let banks, governments and companies run AI on their own servers ('sovereign AI'). The benchmarks are Mistral's own, and on its human-preference coding test it still ranks behind a closed leader (Claude Opus 5.5).

European banks and governments wanting self-hosted AI (our judgment)
research.watch: Independent benchmark results and the promised technical report.
research.eli10: A French company shared its giant AI so anyone can run it on their own computers instead of renting it.

3 yr (our judgment): Open models close more of the gap to closed ones
5 yr (our judgment): Most firms mix open and closed models

research.title: RBI presses banks to prove cyber defences as AI-assisted API attacks hit Indian lenders
research.who: Reserve Bank of India (per Reuters sources)
research.found: Reuters, citing three people familiar with the matter, reports the RBI asked banks to probe weaknesses in APIs, the software links to non-bank lenders and fintechs, and to show proof of compliance and readiness for AI-related risks. Two Mumbai non-bank lenders lost about $2 million in more than 700 unauthorised instant transfers on Oct 8-9 after hackers compromised an API link to ICICI Bank, according to a police complaint. SBI said data of 3,900 customers leaked. CERT-In warned on Oct 9 that hackers steal banks' API credentials, possibly with AI tools.
research.analogy: Like a housing society discovering thieves are coming in through the service lift that delivery partners use, so the guard now checks every partner's key card.
research.brief: Banks connect to fintechs and non-bank lenders through APIs, and smaller partners are 'softer targets'. RBI already has cyber rules, but sources say banks lag in applying them. This is based on unnamed sources, not an official RBI circular.
win: Large banks with bigger security budgets (our judgment)
research.watch: Any formal RBI circular or penalties, and banks' disclosures on cyber spending.
research.eli10: Hackers are sneaking money out through the digital doors banks share with apps, so India's central bank is telling banks to lock those doors better.

3 yr (our judgment): Higher bank cybersecurity spending
5 yr (our judgment): AI-versus-AI fraud defence becomes standard

research.title: A wireless brain implant for artificial vision goes into a third blind patient
research.who: Illinois Tech (lead) with Rush University Medical Center and partners
research.found: Rush surgeons implanted the Intracortical Visual Prosthesis (ICVP) in a third participant: 34 wireless stimulators carrying 544 electrodes in total, placed in the brain's vision area. It bypasses the eye and optic nerve. The study tests whether people who went blind as adults can use it to move around and do simple visually guided tasks, following each person for one to three years.
research.analogy: Like a stadium light board: each electrode switches on one bulb, and a pattern of bulbs draws a rough picture even when the TV camera (the eye) is broken.
research.brief: Most sight aids need a working optic nerve. ICVP talks directly to the visual cortex, with fully implanted wireless parts. It is an early study with three people so far, and no results on what they can see have been published yet.
research.watch: Published results on what participants can see and do.
research.eli10: Doctors put tiny wireless parts in a blind person's brain that may let them see dots of light to help them get around.

3 yr (our judgment): Larger trial if results hold
5 yr+ (our judgment): Possible path toward device approval

research.title: AtlasBase unveils 'Thalia', a DNA-writing chip with 5.6 billion sites, 700× earlier chips
research.found: AtlasBase announced a molecular computing platform built on Thalia, a CMOS chip with 5.6 billion electrochemical sites that write synthetic DNA. It calls this a 700-fold scale-up over earlier DNA synthesis chips. The platform targets archiving data in DNA and DNA-based computing for search and optimisation problems. Early-access programmes are open to selected partners.
research.analogy: Like going from one printing press to a newspaper plant with billions of tiny presses printing side by side.
research.brief: Writing DNA is the slowest and costliest step of DNA storage. A chip made on standard semiconductor lines could cut cost through massive parallel writing. No write speed, cost per gigabyte or error rate was disclosed.
win: Media and archive owners needing century-scale storage (our judgment)
research.watch: Published write speed, cost per gigabyte and first named customers.
research.eli10: A company built a computer chip that can write billions of DNA strands at once, a step toward saving files in DNA.

research.title: HKU's 'Gungnir' code recovers data from DNA damaged like 400-year-old archives
research.who: The University of Hong Kong (Faculty of Engineering)
research.found: A blockchain-inspired error-correction method uses computing power to guess and verify the original data. It tolerates error rates up to 20%, which HKU calls a fourfold improvement, and recovered data losslessly from DNA damaged to the level expected after about 400 years.
research.analogy: Like rebuilding a torn, faded letter by trying millions of guesses and checking each against a fingerprint until one fits.
research.brief: DNA can hold huge amounts of data for centuries, but the molecules decay and reading them adds errors. Gungnir moves the burden to computers: more compute, stronger repair. Lab and computational result; writing DNA is still slow and costly.

Archive and cloud storage providers (our judgment)
research.watch: Independent tests and use with a commercial DNA-writing system.
research.eli10: Scientists store files in DNA. This trick fixes the file even when the DNA gets very old and broken.

3 yr (our judgment): Pilot archives may test it
5 yr (our judgment): Could become a standard layer if DNA writing gets cheap

research.title: DNA-SaM: a DNA storage system tested in the lab and in living cells with 100% recovery
research.who: Research team publishing in Nature Communications
research.found: DNA-SaM combines fast encoding, checks that avoid problem DNA sequences, and a two-level index for large files. It was validated in vitro and in vivo with a 100% success rate and could theoretically hold more than 270 petabytes.
research.analogy: Like a library that labels every shelf and refuses to print pages that would jam the photocopier.
research.brief: Most DNA-storage codecs are slow or create sequences that break lab steps. DNA-SaM targets scale: linear-time encoding and an index for big archives. Capacity is theoretical.
win: DNA synthesis and sequencing toolmakers (our judgment)
research.watch: Real-world archives beyond lab test files.
research.eli10: It is a smart filing system for storing computer files inside DNA, so even huge collections can be found again.
tm: 1 yr (our judgment): Benchmarked against other codecs
3 yr (our judgment): Used in larger lab demos
5 yr (our judgment): Part of a DNA-archive product stack if costs fall
bear: The 270 PB figure is a theoretical capacity, not data actually stored

research.title: A porous silica chip writes 11× more DNA per spot, a step to cheaper 'DNA drives'
research.who: Research team publishing in Microsystems & Nanoengineering
research.found: A porous silica thin film raises on-chip DNA yield to more than 1,821 pmol per cm², over 11 times a flat surface, using chip-making-compatible electrochemistry. The team wrote and recovered digital data with error rates comparable to other lab systems.
research.analogy: Like turning a flat parking lot into a multi-storey garage: same footprint, many more cars.
research.brief: Writing DNA is the costliest step in DNA storage. Electrochemical chips pack many write sites but each site makes little DNA. A porous surface boosts yield per site while staying compatible with semiconductor processes.
research.watch: Scaling to dense arrays and longer strands.
research.eli10: Making DNA for storage is slow. This chip has tiny sponge-like holes, so each spot makes much more DNA.
tm: 1 yr (our judgment): Follow-up with denser arrays
3 yr (our judgment): Prototype DNA-writing chips
5 yr (our judgment): Could cut DNA-write cost if paired with fab partners
bear: Demonstrated with 121-letter strands in a lab-built system

research.analogy: Like a kitchen that can finally make a rare spice in-house instead of waiting for costly imports; every complex recipe needs it.

research.watch: Cultivation at larger scale and inside a full logical computation.

research.brief: Many studies use only 10 to 20 qubits on bigger chips. Using the full chip matters for real workloads. The fidelity is only just above the threshold.
research.watch: Full-chip results on useful algorithms, not just benchmarks.

research.title: First prime edit inside a human body: Prime Medicine treats a Wilson's disease patient
research.found: Prime Medicine treated the first person in a trial that uses prime editing to rewrite DNA in liver cells, aiming to fix a mutation that stops them clearing excess copper. First results are expected next year.
research.analogy: Classic CRISPR is scissors; prime editing is find-and-replace in a word processor.
research.brief: No gene-editing therapy is yet approved for use inside the body. Base editing cannot fix the most common Wilson's mutations; prime editing can insert, delete and rewrite. Nature reports the FDA expects to decide early next year on an in-body CRISPR therapy for hereditary angioedema.
